summary.text: 花 means “flower” and is constructed as a phonosemantic character: 艹 marks the plant category, while 化 provides a similar-sounding cue. Tang citations attest the flower and “to flower” uses; the graph’s first appearance is unresolved.

formation.text: The later graph combines a plant-category element, 艹, with 化 as a probable sound element. Mandarin huā and huà are similar, and Old Chinese reconstructions also show a partial sound match, though they do not directly record ancient speech or date the graph’s formation.

components.text: 艹 is the plant-category element in 花. It is a conventional side form of 艸, not evidence here of a separate historical stage.

化 serves as a probable sound element in 花. Mandarin 花 huā and 化 huà are similar but differ in tone and vowel; Baxter–Sagart reconstructions share a similar onset and medial sequence but differ in their ending.

sound.text: Mandarin 花 huā and 化 huà are similar, though their tones and vowels differ.

In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstructions, 花 *qʷʰˤra and 化 *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s share a similar onset and medial sequence but differ in the ending. These are reconstructed forms, not direct records of ancient speech.

history.text: A modern seal-script-style drawing presents 花 in a later script style; it is not an ancient artifact or a dated step in the graph’s development.

The received Shuowen analysis treats 𠌶 as the flower of grasses and trees, composed of 𠂹 and phonetic 亏, and 華 as flourishing, composed of 艸 and 𠌶. A modern paleographic proposal instead sees a plant and flower in early 𠌶 and 于 as its sound element, suggesting that later graphic alteration made the flower strokes resemble 𠂹. These analyses conflict, and neither establishes a continuous graphic sequence into 花.

Dictionaries describe 花 as a later form associated with 華 and using 化 for sound. Tang citations attest 花 in use, but the date when this graph arose and its precise graphic connection with 𠌶 or 華 remain unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The supplied evidence identifies no oracle-bone form or primary dated first occurrence of 花. The seal-style drawing does not establish the graph’s earliest formation.

化 is a plausible sound element, supported by component analyses and reconstructed comparisons. Those comparisons are not ancient recordings and do not establish when 花 was formed or its exact original pronunciation.
The received Shuowen analysis of 𠌶 conflicts with a modern proposal that it depicts a plant and flower and contains phonetic 于; the graphic history remains disputed.

senses.period: Tang citations; earlier first use of 花 unresolved
senses.text: Tang citations attest 花 for the noun “flower.” The older graphs 𠌶 and 華 have flower-related definitions or reported uses, but those do not establish an early attestation of 花 itself.
A Tang citation attests 花 as a verb meaning “to flower.” The evidence does not establish when this use arose relative to the noun.

senses.gloss: flower-like objects and other figurative or extended senses
senses.text: Later recorded senses include flower-like objects, beauty, patterns, and expenditure. Their dates and paths of development from “flower” are unresolved.

developments.text: Both noun and verb uses are attested, but the evidence does not establish that one developed from the other or show their chronology.

limitations.text: The first use of 花 as a graph is unresolved, as are the chronology of the noun and verb uses and the semantic paths to later figurative meanings.

evidence.text: A flower 艹 in bloom 化; 化 also provides the pronunciation
Phonosemantic compound. 艹 represents the meaning and 化 represents the sound.

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *hʷraː): semantic 艹 (“grass; plant”) + phonetic 化 (OC *hŋʷraːls). Originally 𠌶 or 華 before the Han dynasty.
Unclear.
Possibly of Sino-Tibetan origin. Schuessler (2007) derives it from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *baːr (“bloom, flower”) and thus an example of possible *b ~ *w variation, with final -r moved to medial position. If so, cognate with 葩 (MC phae); outside Sinitic, compare Burmese ပန်း (pan:), Lepcha ᰓᰫᰲ (búr), Mizo páar, etc. Sagart (2021) also connects it to 葩 (OC *pʰˤra), modifying Baxter and Sagart's (2014) reconstruction to *Cə-pʰˤra and proposing the sound changes *Cə-pʰ- > *Cə-ɸ- > *ɸ- > xw-.
Sagart & Baxter (2024) reconstruct 荂 (OC *pʰra) ~ 葩 (OC *pʰˤra) and 荂 (OC *X.pʰra) ~ 花 (OC *X.pʰˤra) (with unknown prefix *X turning labial stops into Middle Chinese fricative initials in 荂 (MC xju) ~ 花 (MC xwae)) (which might have already happened by the time of the Western Zhou dynasty, as shown by the presence of the 于 (OC *ɢʷa) radical in its earliest form 𦻏). Furthermore, they propose cognacy to Proto-Karen *phɔᴬ (“flower”) and reconstruct Proto-Sino-Tibetan *p(h)a (“idem”). Outside Sino-Tibetan, they propose cognacy to Proto-Austronesian *pahpah (“flower, petal; leaf”).
Alternatively, from Austroasiatic; compare Proto-Austroasiatic *bka(ː)ʔ (“flower”) (Schuessler, 2007).
華 (OC *ɡʷraː, “to flower”) is a derivative.

evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi, text hosted by Wikisource
evidence.text: The received Shuowen text defines 𠌶 as the flower of grasses and trees and analyzes it as 𠂹 plus 亏 as phonetic; it defines 華 as flourishing and analyzes it as 艸 plus 𠌶. This records the Han-period lexicographic analysis, not independent proof of the graphs’ original design.
evidence.title: 說文解字/06

evidence.source: Li Guisen and Liu Hongtao, “釋‘華’及相關諸字,” Tsinghua University Research Center for Excavated Texts
evidence.field: paleographic analysis of 𠌶 and 𠂹
evidence.text: The authors challenge the Shuowen analysis: their reading of bronze and Warring States forms identifies 于 as the phonetic element of 𠌶 and interprets the upper portion as a plant with a flower. They argue that later graphic alteration made the flower strokes resemble 𠂹, leading Shuowen to misanalyze the graph. They describe early bronze forms as having plant-like and pictorial features, while emphasizing the phonetic 于. This is a scholarly proposal, not an uncontested account.
evidence.title: 釋“華”及相關諸字

evidence.source: Tsinghua University Research Center for Excavated Texts, article contents page
evidence.text: The center lists Li Guisen and Liu Hongtao’s study in 出土文獻第五輯, supporting its identity and publication context. The study discusses examples from bronze inscriptions and Warring States manuscripts; some graph forms in the PDF are not rendered in the extracted text, so they were not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 甲骨金文研究—清华大学出土文献研究与保护中心

evidence.text: The entry reports Shuowen’s account of 𠌶, gives the alternative form 荂, and lists named Western Zhou bronze examples including 命簋, 不栺方鼎, 𧻷盂, 仲姞鬲, and 仲義父鼎. This is a secondary compilation of dated paleographic references; it does not establish an oracle-bone form for the character.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Variant Chinese Character Dictionary
evidence.field: 花 entry; historical citations and headword note
evidence.text: The dictionary says 花 is not recorded as a headword in Shuowen and identifies it as a correct character as well as a variant of 華. Its citations include Tang texts for the senses ‘flower’ and ‘to flower’; it also notes the Song Jiyun’s 花/華 forms and fanqie 呼瓜切. The citations establish these later recorded uses, not the date of the character’s first use.
evidence.title: A03439 花 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.field: historical usage citations and historical commentary
evidence.text: The entry cites the Han Shu annotation to 張衡傳, which says 蘤 was an old graph for 花 and that canonical texts generally used 華. It also records the later use of 花 in Du Fu and Bai Juyi. A historical commentary reproduced on the page argues that 花 is absent from pre-Northern/Southern Dynasties books and occurs in texts from Jin onward, sometimes through later textual alteration. These are distinct source assertions; the inspected page does not resolve the earliest actual occurrence of the graph 花.
evidence.title: 花 huā - 漢典

evidence.text: The entry distinguishes the plant’s flower, flowering plants, flower-like objects, metaphorical beauty, and several later figurative senses. Its citation for 花 ‘to flower’ is Du Fu; it provides no dated chain proving when or how the later figurative senses developed.
evidence.title: 花 huā - 漢典

evidence.source: 漢典, phonology page for 花
evidence.text: The page records 花 in Guangyun with fanqie 呼瓜切, level tone, 麻 rhyme, and its own transcription xua. That is a Middle Chinese rhyme-book record, distinct from a reconstruction of Old Chinese.
evidence.title: 花的音韻方言

evidence.text: The entry asserts a phonosemantic analysis of 花 as 艹 meaning plus 化 sound and says the word was originally written 華. It lists Mandarin huā, Middle Chinese xwae, and Old Chinese *qʷʰˤra. This is a modern summary; its page does not give dated primary evidence for when 花 was formed or for each semantic extension.
evidence.title: 花 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.text: The entry gives 化 as Mandarin huà and Old Chinese *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s, Middle Chinese xwaeH, gloss ‘transform’; it also lists 花 among graphs in which 化 functions as a sound component. In Baxter–Sagart notation, this reconstructed 化 reading is not identical to the flower reading *qʷʰˤra, but shares a similar onset and medial sequence. These are reconstructions rather than directly attested ancient pronunciations.
evidence.title: 化 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1
evidence.text: The retrieved reconstruction table gives 化 ‘transform’ as *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s, Middle Chinese xwaeH, under the Baxter–Sagart system. Its relevance here is comparison of the alleged sound component’s reading with 花; it does not document the component assignment itself.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 花 historical phonology and readings

evidence.source: Tsinghua University study, discussion of 荂 and 華
evidence.field: Warring States orthographic and textual examples
evidence.text: The authors report Warring States manuscript uses of 芋 as 華, including examples in Chu manuscripts, and interpret contexts such as 裳裳者芋 as referring to 華 in the Book of Odes. This supports the use of 華-related forms for flower/flourishing meanings and cautions against treating 花 as the sole old spelling. The semantic and orthographic relation is argued from manuscript context; it does not make 花’s graphic history identical to that of 華.
evidence.title: 釋“華”及相關諸字

evidence.field: glyph origin; component analysis; Old Chinese comparisons
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 花 as 艹 (plant/grass) plus 化 (phonetic), and says earlier flower graphs included 𠌶 or 華 before Han. In Zhengzhang’s reconstruction, 花 is *hʷraː and 化 is *hŋʷraːls. This is a modern account, not direct proof of when 花 was formed.

evidence.field: research note on 花 and its related forms
evidence.text: The entry says Shuowen lacks a 花 headword and records 𠌶 and 華; it presents later 花 as a form using 化 for sound. It also cites Wang Niansun’s view that an older form was written with 艸 and 白, and that its sound was like 化. This is a dictionary’s account of prior scholarship; it does not settle the earliest use of the 花 graph.

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction
evidence.field: Old Chinese and Middle Chinese readings for 花, 華, and 化
evidence.text: In the Baxter–Sagart system, the table gives 花 ‘flower’ as Mandarin huā, Middle Chinese xwae, Old Chinese *qʷʰˤra; 化 ‘transform’ as huà, xwaeH, *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s. evidence.text: The entry distinguishes the plant’s flower, flowering plants, flower-like objects, metaphorical beauty, and several later figurative senses. Its citation for 花 ‘to flower’ is Du Fu; it provides no dated chain proving when or how the later figurative senses developed.
evidence.title: 花 huā - 漢典

evidence.source: 漢典, phonology page for 花
evidence.text: The page records 花 in Guangyun with fanqie 呼瓜切, level tone, 麻 rhyme, and its own transcription xua. That is a Middle Chinese rhyme-book record, distinct from a reconstruction of Old Chinese.
evidence.title: 花的音韻方言

evidence.text: The entry asserts a phonosemantic analysis of 花 as 艹 meaning plus 化 sound and says the word was originally written 華. It lists Mandarin huā, Middle Chinese xwae, and Old Chinese *qʷʰˤra. This is a modern summary; its page does not give dated primary evidence for when 花 was formed or for each semantic extension.
evidence.title: 花 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.text: The entry gives 化 as Mandarin huà and Old Chinese *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s, Middle Chinese xwaeH, gloss ‘transform’; it also lists 花 among graphs in which 化 functions as a sound component. In Baxter–Sagart notation, this reconstructed 化 reading is not identical to the flower reading *qʷʰˤra, but shares a similar onset and medial sequence. These are reconstructions rather than directly attested ancient pronunciations.
evidence.title: 化 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1
evidence.text: The retrieved reconstruction table gives 化 ‘transform’ as *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s, Middle Chinese xwaeH, under the Baxter–Sagart system. Its relevance here is comparison of the alleged sound component’s reading with 花; it does not document the component assignment itself.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (20 September 2014)

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 花 historical phonology and readings
evidence.text: The page reports Mandarin huā, Cantonese faa1, Japanese kun reading hana, Japanese on readings ka/ke, Korean hwa, Vietnamese hoa; its cited Middle Chinese reconstructions include Baxter xwae and Zhengzhang hˠua. It lists 花 as Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese *qʷʰˤra and Zhengzhang Old Chinese *hʷraː, identifying 化 as a phonetic component in its Zhengzhang table. The systems differ, and these database entries are not independent primary evidence for formation.
evidence.title: 花 - 維基詞典，自由的多語言詞典

evidence.source: Tsinghua University study, discussion of 荂 and 華
evidence.field: Warring States orthographic and textual examples
evidence.text: The authors report Warring States manuscript uses of 芋 as 華, including examples in Chu manuscripts, and interpret contexts such as 裳裳者芋 as referring to 華 in the Book of Odes. This supports the use of 華-related forms for flower/flourishing meanings and cautions against treating 花 as the sole old spelling. The semantic and orthographic relation is argued from manuscript context; it does not make 花’s graphic history identical to that of 華.
evidence.title: 釋“華”及相關諸字

evidence.field: glyph origin; component analysis; Old Chinese comparisons
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 花 as 艹 (plant/grass) plus 化 (phonetic), and says earlier flower graphs included 𠌶 or 華 before Han. In Zhengzhang’s reconstruction, 花 is *hʷraː and 化 is *hŋʷraːls. This is a modern account, not direct proof of when 花 was formed.
evidence.title: 花 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: research note on 花 and its related forms
evidence.text: The entry says Shuowen lacks a 花 headword and records 𠌶 and 華; it presents later 花 as a form using 化 for sound. It also cites Wang Niansun’s view that an older form was written with 艸 and 白, and that its sound was like 化. This is a dictionary’s account of prior scholarship; it does not settle the earliest use of the 花 graph.
evidence.title: [A03439-004] (花) - Ministry of Education《Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants》

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction
evidence.field: Old Chinese and Middle Chinese readings for 花, 華, and 化
evidence.text: In the Baxter–Sagart system, the table gives 花 ‘flower’ as Mandarin huā, Middle Chinese xwae, Old Chinese *qʷʰˤra; 化 ‘transform’ as huà, xwaeH, *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s. The authors explain that use of 化 as a phonetic element in 華 flower reflects a Han-period merger of Old Chinese *-raj and *-ra in syllables with pharyngealized onsets. The reconstructions are comparative proposals, not directly recorded ancient pronunciations.
evidence.title: Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction

evidence.text: The page describes a digital vector drawing of 花 in Shuowen seal-script style and points to source databases, including the Sinica Database and Chinese Etymology. It says this particular image is from S04460 on the 華 entry and gives public-domain terms for the SVG representation. This is a modern redraw of a historical script form, not an artifact photograph.

evidence.text: The entry says 花 is not recorded in Shuowen. It gives modern Mandarin huā and quotes Tang examples for the noun ‘flower’ (段成式, 崔護) and verb ‘to flower’ (杜甫). Its further senses include flower-like objects, beauty, patterns, variety, expenditure, and others, but the displayed citations do not establish a dated chain linking those extensions.
evidence.title: A03439 花 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Wikisource, received text of Shuowen Jiezi
evidence.text: The received Shuowen text defines 𠌶 as the flower of grasses and trees, analyzing it as 从𠂹亏聲; 華 is defined as flourishing and analyzed as 从艸从𠌶. This is the Han-period lexicographic analysis, not independent proof of original graphic design.
evidence.title: 說文解字/06

evidence.source: Li Guisen and Liu Hongtao, Tsinghua University Research Center for Excavated Texts
evidence.text: The authors argue that early forms depict a plant and open flower, with graphic simplification and later alteration making the flower strokes resemble 𠂹. They propose that Shuowen consequently misanalyzed the form. This is their scholarly interpretation; it conflicts with Shuowen’s account and should not be stated as settled fact.
evidence.title: 釋“華”及相關諸字

evidence.source: Li Guisen and Liu Hongtao, Tsinghua University Research Center for Excavated Texts
evidence.field: Warring States uses and graphic relations among 華 forms
evidence.text: The authors report Warring States manuscript 芋 used for 華, including flower/flourishing contexts. They propose that 華 developed from a flower graph with an added 艸 classifier, and discuss 春秋-period 華 examples. Their account distinguishes these graphs from later 花; it does not demonstrate a continuous sequence into 花.
evidence.title: 釋“華”及相關諸字

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: research note on 花 and related forms
evidence.text: The dictionary reports that Shuowen has entries for 𠌶 and 華 but not 花, and describes later 花 as using 化 for sound. It also reports Wang Niansun’s analysis of an older variant with 艸 and 白 whose sound was like 化. These are dictionary summaries of historical scholarship, not a dated first attestation of 花.
evidence.title: A03439 花 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 韻典網, Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese phonology database
evidence.field: 花 phonetic-series assignment and comparative readings
evidence.text: The entry assigns 花 to phonetic 化 and gives Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese hʷraː, with Middle Chinese comparisons including xwa (Karlgren and Wang Li), xua (Li Rong and Shao Rongfen), hɣua (Zhengzhang), hʷɯa (Pan Wuyun), and hwaɨ (Pulleyblank). These are reconstructions or transcriptions in their named systems, not ancient recordings.

evidence.text: The page gives Mandarin huā and reconstructions Baxter–Sagart *qʷʰˤra and Zhengzhang *hʷraː; it identifies 化 as the sound component in its Zhengzhang table. Together with the separate 化 comparison in the dossier, this supports a plausible later sound-component analysis. Because the systems differ and the available independent 化 comparison is not a primary attestation, this does not establish the graph’s date or exact original pronunciation.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The earliest attested forms concern 𠌶/華-related graphs; the sources inspected do not establish an oracle-bone form for 花, and the bronzes listed for 𠌶 were not visually inspected.

The traditional Shuowen analysis (𠌶 from 𠂹, with 亏 phonetic) conflicts with the Tsinghua study’s reading of an earlier plant/flower pictorial portion and 于 phonetic. The precise graphic transition and the status of alleged corruption remain disputed.

The relationship of 華 to the later 花 graph is described by modern dictionaries as an older spelling/variant, but the exact date when 花 arose and whether it first functioned as a phonosemantic graph are not settled by the inspected primary evidence.

The distinction between the early spoken flower word and the later graph 花 requires caution: early flower uses commonly appear as 華 or related graphs; no independently verified first textual token of 花 was located. The record reports competing claims ranging from Jin-period attestations to later dictionary recognition.

花 and 化 are both Mandarin huā/huà respectively. Under Baxter–Sagart (2014), flower 花 is *qʷʰˤra and transform 化 is *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s; under Zhengzhang, 花 is *hʷraː. These comparisons make a sound-component analysis plausible but do not independently date the formation of 花.
Older compound graphs 𠌶 and 華 have different component histories from later 花. Do not transfer the 艹+化 analysis to those earlier forms.

Later meanings such as flower-like object, beauty, pattern, variegation, expenditure, or indistinctness are listed in dictionaries, but the inspected sources do not establish the dates or semantic bridges for most of them.
Broader Sino-Tibetan/Austroasiatic/Austronesian comparisons in the dossier were not independently checked against the underlying comparative studies and are not included as established findings.
Search snippets were not treated as inspected page contents. The Baxter–Sagart PDF open attempt failed internally; only the indexed table row was available.

The fresh search did not establish a primary dated token for the first use of 花 as a graph, nor settle conflicting accounts of its formation date. The earlier 𠌶/華 and later 花 histories must remain distinct.
The entry and reconstruction source support 艹 as semantic and 化 as phonetic in the later graph, but do not independently establish a full dated sequence of graphic change from 𠌶/華 to 花.

The Zhengzhang and Baxter–Sagart values are reconstructions from different systems and should not be conflated. This search did not inspect an independent original reconstruction dataset for Zhengzhang.
No dated chain for semantic extensions beyond ‘flower’ was established in this fresh check.
No Xiaoxuetang form record or reusable specific 𠌶/華 artifact image was located. The candidate image below is a modern redraw in seal-script style, not an ancient artifact photograph.
No source in this search claims a whole-graph phonetic loan for 花; the sound analysis concerns 化 as a component, so no depicted tool or object name is required.
No primary dated first occurrence of the graph 花 was established. The MOE entry supplies Tang citations for flower and flowering senses, while secondary accounts differ on when 花 emerged.

The received Shuowen analysis of 𠌶 differs from the Tsinghua study’s proposed flower depiction and account of graphic alteration. The Tsinghua paper provides a scholarly alternative, not a settled correction.

The relation of later 花 to older 𠌶/華 is reported as spelling or variant history, but the inspected sources do not establish an uninterrupted dated graphic sequence. Component roles in the later 花 graph must not be transferred to those older forms.

化’s role as sound component is supported by modern dictionaries and a Zhengzhang-series database, but no independently inspected primary reconstruction table for 化 was obtained in this search. Historical reconstructions are theoretical comparisons, not direct ancient pronunciations.
Tang attestations support flower and ‘to flower’; dates and semantic links for later senses such as spending, pattern, beauty, and indistinctness remain unestablished here.
